profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting is a design review for an internal proposal describing an LLVM-based optimization pipeline for SPDZ that compiles a privacy-annotated subset of C into LLVM IR, applies protocol-aware batching and scheduling, and targets both CPU and optional GPU execution for the online phase. The context is that the team wants to decide whether the current design doc is ready to circulate to the broader cryptography and systems group before implementation is expanded beyond proof-of-concept benchmarks. The agenda is to review whether the proposal is 'ready', whether the described evaluation and scheduler boundaries are sufficient for sign-off, and what edits are needed around the runtime, GPU path, and comparison to MP-SPDZ. The expected outcome is a go-ahead to revise the design doc with a short list of changes rather than reopening the architecture.

members.name: Priya Raman
members.expertise: LLVM optimization passes, IR lowering, static analysis, performance-oriented compiler infrastructure
members.background: Priya joined from a systems compiler team where she built optimization pipelines over LLVM for domain-specific runtimes, and she now leads the compiler side of the MPC tooling effort.
members.private_state: Priya wants the review to conclude that the architecture is stable enough to publish internally, because her team needs approval to keep the IR and pass interfaces fixed while they implement more optimizations; she is worried that opening up online/runtime details too much will trigger a broader redesign request.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says 'SPDZ pipeline', reviewers will understand it as an optimization layer over the online execution path, not a full protocol implementation including offline preprocessing.
A design being 'ready' for review means the IR contract, pass boundaries, and runtime interfaces are stable, even if benchmarking methodology and deployment details are still lightweight.
The 'GPU back end' is naturally understood as optional code generation for batched arithmetic kernels once the scheduler has already formed batches on the host.
References to 'the baseline' in the doc will be read as the MP-SPDZ microbenchmark setup used in the current experiments, not as a production-equivalent full-stack comparison.

members.name: Ethan Cole
members.expertise: MPC protocol engineering, SPDZ deployments, runtime architecture, secure systems evaluation
members.background: Ethan has led several internal integrations of MP-SPDZ-style systems into privacy-preserving analytics services and usually reviews designs for operational completeness rather than pure compiler elegance.
members.private_state: Ethan wants to approve the proposal if it will not create downstream confusion for protocol engineers, but he is concerned about designs that look complete while leaving practical runtime assumptions unstated; he prefers not to block the team over wording if the missing pieces are merely documentation gaps.
hidden_assumptions: When someone presents a 'SPDZ design', it implicitly includes enough treatment of the offline/online handoff, preprocessed material availability, and runtime constraints that protocol engineers could reason about end-to-end integration.
A design being 'ready' means it is ready for broader architecture review with evaluation claims framed tightly enough that other groups would not misread benchmark scope or deployment implications.
The 'GPU back end' naturally includes the execution path details needed to move secret-shared tensors and associated metadata through the runtime, not just kernel emission after batching.

References to 'the baseline' will be interpreted by most reviewers as MP-SPDZ in the closest realistic configuration to the proposed system, including comparable runtime overheads and execution conditions.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the SPDZ pipeline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the design 'covers the SPDZ pipeline' and focuses on the 'online phase'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the compiler plus scheduler for online arithmetic execution only, assuming offline preprocessing and correlated randomness are external inputs and therefore out of scope for this review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan means the document should at least specify the interface and assumptions around the offline/online boundary so the pipeline can be understood as a usable SPDZ system component rather than an isolated execution engine.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both accept that the main performance gains are in the online phase, saying 'we focus on online' sounds fully aligned; neither feels the need to restate whether offline integration details are merely assumed or intentionally omitted.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the design doc is 'ready to circulate' or 'ready for broader review'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya thinks readiness means the architecture, IR boundaries, and key optimization story are stable enough that reviewers can react to the intended design without demanding implementation-complete details.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan thinks readiness means outside reviewers will not be able to misread the system scope, benchmark claims, or deployment assumptions because the document already pins down those contextual details.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'ready' is a routine approval phrase and both are cooperative; they each assume the other is using the common team standard, so surface agreement on minor edits masks different thresholds for completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: What the GPU back end includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the GPU back end' as an optional extension of the design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya uses 'GPU back end' to mean lowering already-formed batched arithmetic operations into GPU kernels and launching them from the host scheduler.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan uses 'GPU back end' to mean the broader execution path needed for GPU use in SPDZ, including buffer staging, secret-share layout movement, synchronization assumptions, and runtime interaction costs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'GPU back end' is standard enough to sound precise, and both genuinely believe they are using accepted systems terminology; the missing distinction between code generation and full execution plumbing is second-order and easy to leave implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: Which MP-SPDZ baseline is being reviewed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both mention 'the MP-SPDZ baseline' when discussing evaluation language.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is thinking of the team's current controlled microbenchmark harness against MP-SPDZ's CPU online execution path with matching arithmetic kernels and no attempt to replicate broader application-level runtime conditions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan is thinking of the nearest deployment-relevant MP-SPDZ configuration reviewers are likely to imagine, including full runtime behavior and enough surrounding conditions to infer practical integration value.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Since both know the project already uses MP-SPDZ as the named comparator, saying 'the baseline' feels unambiguous; neither notices they are anchoring on different concrete instantiations of that baseline.

turns.inner_thought: I want to frame this as a narrow architecture readiness check, not an invitation to reopen protocol scope. The core is stable: privacy-annotated C lowers into LLVM IR, the batching and scheduling passes are defined, and the runtime hooks for online execution are clear enough for my team to keep building. If we can leave this meeting with agreement that the SPDZ pipeline design is ready to circulate after a few edits, we can freeze the IR and pass interfaces and avoid getting dragged into a broader redesign around offline machinery.

From my side, the architecture is in good shape; I mostly want to make sure the boundaries read clearly enough for broader review.

turns.inner_thought: The direction looks reasonable, and I don't want to block them over presentation issues if the gaps are just document gaps. But when something says SPDZ design and ready for broader review, people from protocol engineering will read it end to end and infer operational assumptions whether or not they're written. I need to check that the boundaries, evaluation framing, and runtime expectations are stated tightly enough that nobody mistakes a proof-of-concept compiler path for a complete deployable architecture.
turns.utterance: Overall, the direction makes sense to me. My comments are mostly about whether it's ready for broader review in a way that keeps readers aligned on the system boundaries. If we can make those assumptions explicit enough, I think this is in a good place.

The proposal is intentionally about accelerating the online phase: front end to LLVM IR, protocol-aware batching, pass pipeline, then runtime scheduling over arithmetic ops. That's what I mean by covering the SPDZ pipeline here, and I expect Ethan to read 'focus on online' the same way.
